segments.text: I grew up in Miami, um, and I went there when I was very little with my parents. My dad worked for Rolls-Royce USA, um, and so spent all of my childhood in Florida, um, and everybody's moved from Miami now, um, everybody's going further north, um, and when I asked them, like, why is everyone leaving the old neighborhood? Why are you all moving north? And it's basically because there's such a big Cuban influence in Miami now that they feel like they're pushed out and they've got to go north, which is really shocking. Um, but it can be a little bit—

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Hasn't it always kind of been like that though?

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: Well, I don't remember. I remember Cubans when I was younger and we lived there, but I don't remember It being massively, massively, um, Cuban influenced. I think there's been a lot more immigration, and I don't know.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Well, there probably has, yes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: I mean, I don't know, it can be— it's a bit like sometimes you can feel a little bit outnumbered, can't you? I mean, we've got I mean, I'd never, I'd never want to say anything racist, and I wouldn't want to offend anybody, but here in the UK we've got massive, massive Asian communities and whole cities. I mean, basically we've got like Bradford, which is a lovely place to go to, um, and I have no problem with the culture, but you don't— if you drive through Bradford They also, they almost look at you as if you shouldn't be there. It's like, what are you doing here? You know what I mean?

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: What is Bradford?

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: Bradford, it's, it's okay. So in the 1940s, after India and Pakistan were created, um, and, um, we, um, ceded India as an independent nation, Um, people that were living in India and Pakistan, um, were British citizens, and they were offered the chance to come and settle here if they wanted to. And it was also coincidentally at the point after the war when a lot of rebuilding had to be done, so we needed, um, men. A lot of men during the war had been killed. A lot of property had been damaged. Um, a lot of men came over from parts of the empire that were and settled here, um, and, um, became builders, laborers, electricians, rebuilding the country after the war. Um, so we ended up going— we went from this very culturally closed country that had had influences from all around the world. I mean, we'd had several hundred years of empire, so it wasn't that we were without influences, but it was at a distance to it being here. And now a lot of people settled in areas that needed rebuilding. So there's Bradford, Manchester, places where there'd been manufacturing the Germans had bombed. London. So there's traditionally where people have settled, there's these massive communities. And Bradford, people call it Bradistan. It's a massive, massive city. It's a very nice city. It's very well kept. The people appear to be very friendly. But because it is so massive, an Asian community, if you're white and you go into it, you can almost feel like you shouldn't be there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Oh wow, I didn't know all that about the war and stuff. I should brush up on my history.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: It's like we've got massive, massive Chinese communities here as well because, um, Hong Kong was part of Britain, part of the empire, and then it got handed back to China in the '90s. Um, it was rented from China, um, and the rental agreement came to an end, so it was handed back. And people that lived there had British Overseas Territory passports, so they were entitled to come and live here. We've got big Chinese communities. It's like Grand Cayman. That's British. I've got friends in Cayman, and they can come and settle here if they want to. And so it's like when the empire ended, we went from this very white middle, middle upper class society, um, that had had influences from around the world for a couple of hundred years, but it had always been influences. It's like, it's like it was always at a distance, um, and, um, Then there was a massive, massive influx after the war, and all of a sudden these white British people that had gone to church and preached as Christians and whatever— it was very much white Christian background— had to deal with people from, um, places like the Caribbean, India, Pakistan, China. Coming here because they'd got citizenship.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Um, I'm still wondering why you left Miami.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: I left Miami— I'll tell you why I left Miami— because I'd got elderly grandparents that were becoming frail, um, and, um, my mother was an only child, so her parents had only got my mum to look after them. And, um, it was at the point in the '90s where there was a bit of a recession. Rolls-Royce USA, um, shed a lot of its staff. And, um, when Rose— my dad came, he asked about rejoining Rolls-Royce UK, and they were getting rid of staff as well because of a recession. Um, they were making people redundant. My dad would have had to have come back to the UK and renewed his green card. And the mortgage for the house partly was through Rolls-Royce USA. They assisted people that wanted to go out and settle with helping them buy property, buy their houses. So, because obviously if you've never lived in America, you've not got an American credit rating or anything. It would be difficult for you back then to get a mortgage. They sponsored people and helped people get buy property and whatever, but the mortgages were through them. So when Rolls Royce USA started to shed staff, they called all the mortgages in. My parents managed to remortgage with an American company, and we kept the house for a long time after we came back. But we only ever. But Dad would have had to have come back and renewed his green card, and there was no guarantee that because he'd not already got a job in the USA that he would be allowed to go back to work. Much as I love America, Americans are a bit funny about foreigners taking their jobs. So it was just no guarantee that if he came back to the UK and renewed his green card that he would. be able to go back out to the USA and find a job working for an American company. So it was too much of a risk, and Mum and Dad came back. Um, the house was left with a letting company, um, and they kept the house right up until a few years ago. We used to go back because, you know, for holidays and everything, and we'd stay as long as we could on a visitor's visa whenever we went over.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Speaker 9
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But it gave me a lot to think about today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: It's been hard though because I was basically— I was 4 when I went out to the USA. I've got really very few memories of living in Britain before America, with only being 4 when we went out. I went to American schools. I went to an elementary, I went to a high school, Um, and my loyalty lay with America. I've always considered myself as American and that being my home. Um, but I'm not, I'm British. I was just brought up there.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But being British is like American, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: I think a lot of people feel that way, that they're like American because they were maybe raised with a lot of like American kind of culture, like, like on TV and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That, and a lot of us kind of come from over there if you trace your roots. I know a lot of my roots go that direction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: But it doesn't give you the right to live there. It's, um, It was just difficult for my parents when it was a big decision to come back here, and it was very, very difficult to settle here after living over there. It's a different— in a lot of ways America and Britain are very similar, but in a lot of ways we're very different. And the lifestyle that we had living in—

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: The lifestyle that we had living in Miami was nothing like the lifestyle we have here. I mean, it was just, you know, Christmas Day on the beach. Dad had a speedboat. Mum had a Pontiac. You know, Dad had a Chevy truck. You know, we had— we were part of a big church. We went to Central Presbyterian in Miami. And it was a very close community. And it was a nice neighborhood. That we lived in, and everybody was very close. Um, and then coming back to dark, damp, cold Britain, you know, I mean, we had a pool in the backyard. It was just a different life, different life completely. It was a far more—

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I would think so, you know, going from sunny Miami.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: To cold Britain. I mean, it's like I've just stood at my back door and had a cigarette. We're gonna get through— it's gonna freeze tonight. It's Flipping cold. Oh Lord, it is. It's horrible. And it's like there's my friends in Miami. It's like my one of my school friends. He's posting on Facebook. He's like, oh, it's like it's cold. It's cold in Miami. I'm like, you've got no idea what cold is, Craig. Honestly, you know, try spending a winter here. You don't just scrape the ice off your car and. You walk down the sidewalk and you're slipping all over the place, and oh, it's just miserable. I hate it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I was going to get my trash can out of. the road, and there was one of those damn COVID masks laying in my yard, and I don't wear them, so it's not mine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: My dog picked one up the other night when I walked him and started running around with it, and I was just like, oh, for God's sake, you know. He's like sat there like a typical terrier wagging his tail, chewing this COVID mask. That's been around someone's mucky mouth, breathing their germs in, and then he comes in afterwards and he wants to jump up and lick me. I'm like, bleh.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: We got the COVID king himself, D-Day. What's up?

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Yeah, it's kind of interesting to walk into this conversation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: That got the better of me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: What is the, um, what is the context here? What are we, what are we talking about? That's Are we talking about dogs and masks, or what's going on?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: We were talking about the— what were we talking about, Jules? I don't remember.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: Dogs picking up discarded COVID masks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Yeah, that doesn't sound like a good thing. I would— it's unfortunate people can't use a garbage can. I know they're complicated devices, but between a paper mask and a garbage can, it just seems like so many people seem to get confused in this world today.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the cloth mask. How often you think those people wash those masks?

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: So I, I bought, um, I mean, I don't know about anybody in this room having the experience I've had over the last couple years concerning COVID-19, but, um, I did buy one of those like cloth— I think it was called a Vogmask— about a year and a half ago, 2 years ago. And I used it when I was going to physical therapy. I never washed it. They said you could, you could clean it off with you know a wet thing or whatever. Don't wash it in water. I used it for a little while, and then I just went back to using the disposable ones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, when I had to wear one, I just wore a bandana.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Yeah. That's probably part of why there's so much fuzz in the data about the effectiveness of, of masking, is most people— I don't think the problem was ever inherently the masks. I think it was user error. Um, no offense to anybody out there, but, uh, there was just really bad messaging about what was working, what wasn't working, and, um, a lot of confirmation bias due to increasing cases, things like that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Mm-hmm. And a lot of political interference. And so science kind of got lost, and you know, it is what it is. So nobody around here has to wear a mask anymore.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: So we don't even hear—

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: but before you got COVID—

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: what's that, Lazy? Did you have the vaccine before you got COVID?

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Oh no, no, no, no. I, um, So I actually live in the Pacific Northwest, and the first official case in the United States was the hospital that's up the street from me. And the, the, the Life Care Center that was at the center in the beginning, the media firestorm over COVID, there was a bunch of older folks that were getting sick in Kirkland, Washington, where I ran a cocktail bar. And my girlfriend is a registered nurse, an RN. She's now the— she's a boss. But she works at the hospital connected to that life care center. So I didn't stand a fucking chance. I was not vaccinated. I was a 220-pound, very healthy bodybuilder who hiked in the Pacific Northwest and supported everybody around me. And I got on March 10th, a couple days before I was supposed to go and and do a walkthrough of the property I was opening my restaurant in to check out the ventilation and the plumbing with my builders. I, I got a little bit of a fever, very, very light, barely at all. And I thought, oh, you know, COVID was going around just a few nights ago. I was making fun of it all, drinking Coronas, taking Instagram shots of myself, not taking it seriously. And I stopped in where my girlfriend worked and I took a— she checked my temperature and a slight fever. So I said, well, I guess I'm going home today. And a couple of days went by and I just— my throat was getting worse. So I walked or I drove over to the clinic that's right by my house and they said, you can't be here. And they gave me a mask and they sent me up the street to another place. And so I got there. And I waited for— because, you know, everybody was in spacesuits back then and nobody was allowed to go in anywhere. I waited for about 6 hours in a parking lot for them to see me in this clinic to check to see if I had COVID. During that time, I contacted my other doctors at the University of Washington as a backup plan in case I couldn't get in. So I did finally get in, and I was exhausted. I was like, why can I not walk from my truck to the clinic? This is weird. And I got into the clinic and it was like 1 or 2 people allowed at a time. And I ended up seeing a doctor. And at the time I was still part-time bartending while working on getting my business open. So, uh, I got in, she looked me over, she didn't do a test or anything. And she said, yeah, it's not COVID. You don't have that. You haven't been to Japan or China or whatever. And I was like, no. And she's like, it's absolutely not COVID.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: So she sent me home with a doctor's note to go back to work in a bar. So I was like, well, I can't go back anyways. I'm not going to do that. You know, I was running that bar at the time as an operational manager and a bartender. So I got home and I was feeling pretty good, like, oh, I guess I don't have COVID. The doctor told me I didn't. And I get a phone call taking a hot bath. My phone starts ringing, and it's the University of Washington. Remember I said I had a backup planned? Well, they called me up and they said, "Hey, so what's up? You think you might have COVID?" And I said, "Well, no. I just went to a doctor and they told me no." And she goes, "Huh. Well, it sounds like you have the symptoms. So let's do a little question, you know, Q&A with you." So they did it, and she said, and I told her that my partner was a cancer nurse, and back then everybody cared about people, right? They were trying to protect everyone. So they said, well, since you're— you live with a cancer nurse, we're gonna— we're gonna go ahead and test you. So the next day I went in for a test and it came back positive a couple days later. But by that point, I was starting to feel better. I was about 7 days in. I think it was the 17th of March, St. Patty's Day or something like that. I was sitting on my couch talking with my brother. And just feeling a little bit run down, but I stood up and I collapsed, you know, and that was a very, very scary moment for me. I came to and I realized that I had no oxygen in me. I don't know how to explain that feeling, but I managed to fall into my bedroom, get across the hallway, and I called 911 because I couldn't move or function or do anything. And When I, I did that, I mean, it was scary. My heart was pounding. I couldn't think. Uh, the, the firemen showed up with the, with the aid car, um, minutes later. They kept me on the line to make sure I'd stay conscious. And I said, you guys gonna come up and get me? They said, no, we can't come up because you're COVID positive. I was like, fuck, okay. They were like, you got to come downstairs. And I was still pretty much undressed at that point, just trying to eat my breakfast and Got up off the couch and collapsed. So I fell down the stairs, 3 flights of stairs, and they got me at the bottom of the stairs. They checked my oxygen, it was at 84%, and they put me into the back of the aid car and they took me to the hospital for my first, my first check-in at the hospital. That was day 7 or whatever. Anyhow, I was not vaccinated.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: And I went to the hospital, I sat in a COVID ward for about 24 hours with this old guy who's about 90-something years old. He was not in good shape. He was blind. But we talked all night long while he gurgled. And I just sat there thinking, this is going to be it for me. I didn't know what was going on. We were all scared in the beginning. And, and during that time, I found out that his daughter-in-law was in the ICU with COVID And the next morning, They were— they said, we're gonna let you go because you're young. You're a young, healthy guy. You're strong. You're fine. It's already day 8. You're gonna— you're gonna be fine. And, um, so on my way out, I heard, uh, the, the gentleman I'd been talking to all night, the 90-something-year-old. He was on the phone crying because his wife was now symptomatic and she was getting— she was getting brought into the hospital. So his entire family was hospitalized. A little traumatic there moment, but, um, They sent me home. I was still weaker than I'd ever imagined a human could feel. And I got home, um, and I was thinking I was going to be fine. And the next day I woke up and I was sicker than I've ever been in my entire life. The kind of sickness I couldn't lift my hand, I couldn't do anything. My girlfriend's a nurse. She couldn't go to work because of course she'd been exposed to me. And, um, I, I laid in bed for another 2 and a half, almost 3 weeks with 3 different ER visits. Uh, very, very traumatic experience. I lost about 40 pounds laying in bed. My girlfriend bought a bedpan for me. She— I couldn't get up to walk after a few more days, uh, so I was peeing in a cup. And, uh, one of the hospital visits I actually went in, they said that I had had a heart attack, but there was no room in the hospital.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: So since I was young and strong and healthy, they thought I was going to be fine. They sent me on my way and they said— and I was wheeled in a wheelchair. I was wheeled in on this one. And they said, you're going to be fine. And the doctor says you can walk out of here because my tests were showing that my blood, everything was looking okay-ish. So they said, walk out. I said, no, man, I can't. I can't walk. You don't understand. They said, walk out. And this is after they ran something that said I'd had a heart attack. I see. I can't. I can't walk out of here. Oh, yes, you can. The doctor said you can. So I said, all right, because I'm a fucking beast, man. You know, I mean, I'm not going to get into what forged me as a human being in my life, but I push. And I got up and I walked about 6 feet and I collapsed into a table and the nurse screamed for a chair. So they grabbed a chair and then she's like, we got to get you out of here. Basically, they were saying there's no room. So they pushed me out, they wheeled me out in the lobby. The nurse is crying, telling me that she's hoping the best for me. They sit me in front of a TV, which at the time they were just showing a bunch of dead people on TV, and I could barely hold my head up. It was like hanging on my shoulder, it was so bad. And they said, do you have somebody come and pick you up? You know, so yeah, my girlfriend. So she came and picked me up, and it continued. And then on the 1st of April, Early in the morning, after I thought I was getting a little bit better, I woke up at about 1 o'clock in the morning with a heart rate of about 130, and my oxygen was a little bit lower. I think it was for whatever reason. It probably wasn't my lungs at that point. It was just this vascular disease that COVID causes. And so she rolled me over onto my stomach into a prone position. We called the hospital because the entire time I was in bed at home, we were monitoring my, my stuff and sending my data into the hospital. So that was a very traumatic experience to constantly look at, worry about your, your biostats, you know, am I dying? Am I dying? So, um, the, the hospital said, yeah, we're gonna admit him. So there I was, I'd been just wasting away. It was horrible. Now finally they're gonna admit me, and they came up About 3 firemen came up and they had to pick me out of bed. I had no balance, no ability to stand or do anything. And they carried me down the stairs, these 3 men who I was once bigger than, um, and they took me into the hospital. They checked my heart, they did a COVID swab on me, and now my COVID swab was negative, but I was this sick. So I sat for 11 days at the hospital. I won't— I'm I won't waste too much more time with the story here. Sat for 11 more days at the hospital, and I had to relearn how to walk. Uh, it was not fun. Uh, and I— when I say relearn how to walk, all I had to do was be able to walk on a walker for 6 feet, and that took 11 days to learn how to do that. Um, and then I got home, and I just didn't get better. I was like I'd been in the ring with Mike Tyson for 100 years, getting hit in the head. And I was having heart problems. I was having signs of heart failure based on, you know, what my girlfriend could tell as a, as an RN. And, um, I couldn't get in to see any doctors because everything was closed. So I just kind of thought, maybe I'm dying. Who knows? This is this weird plague virus nobody knows anything about. And then I, I happened onto some support groups early on, and I met up with communities of people who were struggling and dealing with the same thing I was dealing with and discovered that this was a phenomenon and that it was not being talked about by the government. And so, you know, got into some advocacy stuff, uh, helped to build a social network, a community of people using like Zoom. We did a 24-hour Zoom for— fuck, man, we're still going. I'm looking at it right now, uh, over 2 and a half years nonstop, 24/7 Zoom for people with this condition who, just like a A never-ending Twitter Space, if you imagine. Um, and then over the course of 2020, I got to a point where I was like, I can kind of walk for 10 minutes, you know. And then I went in for— to the hospital because my cardiologist was getting concerned because they were like, we don't know what this thing is doing. And they did a cardiac MRI, but at the hospital I got sick. And I didn't catch COVID but the sickness gave me pneumonia. Again, which was interesting because I'd never had pneumonia before COVID and they found that my immune system was starting to look like an AIDS patient's immune system. So I kind of recovered a little bit from that over the winter of 2020 and then into 2021, and then I got then Lacey I got the vaccine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Hey, hold on a second. They they have like traces of HIV in the vaccine, don't they?

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: No, absolutely not. And I can get into vaccines if you guys really want, because I've researched and worked with working groups, research communities on this, non-biased. These are, these are people with really a serious interest in the safety of, of this, uh, especially—

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: You don't know what I'm talking about? I, I don't remember where I heard something like involved about like the vaccine or COVID.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I know what you're referring to. Yes, I've heard of that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: Is it that they've been treating it the same as they treat HIV infections with more than— with like triple therapy?

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: No, no. And I can, I can elaborate a little bit on that. So I just wanted, I just wanted to get into the vaccine portion since Lacey was curious about that, and, and it's a fair question. Um, there's a lot of, of bad information and incomplete information on both sides of the fence with the vaccine. And, and so I understand why people don't know a lot about it. Um, but the thing is, is I got the vaccine, and I'll tell you, I'll tell you what, Lacey, I was really unable to do anything until about a few weeks after I got my second dose. And then I started to improve. And other people in my communities, the ones I talked about, had started to improve as well. Not everybody, but enough that it caused a little bit of a buzz. And you started to See it even in, in medical communities. They were saying, oh, vaccine will cure long COVID. And then this whole thing got thrown around social media and it blew up. And it's just, it's not true. It's, it's just not true. But it was a clue that there was something immunologically different going on in our bodies because of the infection.

segments.speaker: Speaker 11
segments.text: So this is exactly what we were saying a little while ago. It's a shame you didn't jump into the room about 3/4 of an hour ago.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: So, um, so anyway, That was my experience, right? And then, and then over the course of 2021, I started physical therapy, a couple of other things, and I started to, and I started to watch other people get better. I started to improve a little bit to the point where I was able to go on a couple of mile walks per day, and I was starting to sleep again, and some of my neuropathy was getting better, and some of the things I won't even talk about, they're just so bad. I mean, I pissed my pants like 4 times in public, you guys. This is not— no, no joke.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Um, anyway, by the end of 2021, you guys, I was feeling like I'm gonna be okay. I'm gonna be okay. I'm gonna be one of these people that heals. And then I got Omicron again, or I got Omicron, you know, COVID again. And I spent the next 10 months in 2022 recovering to get back to my baseline, which I still haven't God. And this time I got my bivalent booster, which a lot of my friends who were very pro-vax refused to get boosted anymore because of the impact the vaccine has had on them. This booster shot kicked my arse, man. It destroyed me. So I'm at about 3 weeks and I'm still, I, I'm still barely functioning and I'm still getting confused doing things and And having a really hard time. I wouldn't call it vax damage the way that it's sort of propelled through social media, but I would call it— I would say that if you have this condition from COVID this hyper-inflammatory, autoinflammatory condition, that anything that triggers the immune system to kind of go crazy, especially if it's antigen-specific like the COVID vaccines, Our bodies are primed. There's certain inflammatory pathways that are primed, especially neurologic, like glial cells and those sort of things. And so when the body lights up, it starts sending out all these inflammatory chemicals and they activate things that shouldn't be activated to protect, you know, the neurologic systems in the body. And so they don't work right. So that's kind of where I'm at. I probably won't be ever getting another Vaccine for this again. I might try the Novavax, but it's probably going to have the same effect on me. And the curious part of this is that there are people that I know that had a hard time with the vaccine that upon their next booster or whatever, it was fine, didn't do anything to them. So it almost seems like a person needs to get over the hump of this inflammatory condition and then they sort of enter the realm of what the average normal immune system is like, and then they can tolerate it in a way that's more similar to what the data shows as far as safety and efficacy. And, and I will say there's a lot of issues with the safety and efficacy because they— those companies have not been totally clear and honest about some of these things.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Speaker 10
segments.text: And we haven't been able to have conversations about the vaccine because of the political political sort of inflammation in the conversation. It just, it's made it difficult to have open, honest conversations about science and about truth. And that's, that's really where we're at.
